original_title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 306: Week 1 – August 2026
title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 306: Week 1 – August 2026
original_summary:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained generally stable at the national level during the first week of August, though provincial-level disparities persisted, with some regions facing more pronounced price pressures than others. While week-on-week price movements were moderate across most monitored commodities, prices remained elevated, reflecting the sustained impact of trade disruptions and high transportation costs. Fuel prices remained high, driven by constrained regional supplies, particularly from Russia, and reduced imports from Central Asia and Iran. While elevated fuel prices continued to keep supply chain and delivery costs high, their pass-through to retail food prices remained moderate during the reporting week.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed a mixed but generally stable trend during the first week of August, with several staple commodities recording slight week-on-week changes. Prices remained elevated compared to historical levels, suggesting that markets continue to be adequately supplied, albeit at higher transportation costs.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and wheat flour prices remained largely unchanged week-on-week but stayed significantly higher year-on-year, reflecting elevated production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Rice prices were largely stable during the week. Nevertheless, rice prices remained substantially above last year and the three-year average, particularly Sholae rice, which is 35% higher year-on-year.

• Other Staples: Prices of cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt showed mixed but generally modest week-on-week movements. Cooking oil increased by 0.9%, while pulses, sugar, and salt declined slightly. Compared to last year, cooking oil, sugar, and salt remained elevated by 12%, 10%, and 9%, respectively, while pulse prices were 13% lower, reflecting relatively favourable availability.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices increased during the first week of August, led by onion and potato prices, which rose by 5.9% and 4.6%, respectively. Compared to last year, tomato and potato prices remained significantly higher, by 30% and 49%, respectively, while onion prices are 7% lower.
Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani exchange rate remained broadly stable at AFN 66.0/USD. Although the currency remained broadly unchanged from last week, it continued to outperform both last year (4% stronger) and the three-year average (11% stronger), helping to partially offset imported inflationary pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices eased slightly during the week but remained 13% above last year and 16% above the three-year average, reflecting continued regional supply constraints and elevated international fuel prices.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices show a slight decline from last week, with DAP price falling by 1.1% and Urea by 2.0%. However, prices remained substantially above last year's levels, with DAP 17% and Urea 42% higher.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep remained stable with moderate week-on-week fluctuations. However, it stood 6% below last year and 2% below the three-year average, reflecting weak pastoralists' terms of trade (purchasing power of livestock keepers).

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued, with labour availability averaging 2.1 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while the daily wage for unskilled labour remained unchanged.

original_title: Somalia - WFP Joint VAM-Supply Chain | Market Bulletin (July 2026)
title: Somalia - WFP Joint VAM-Supply Chain | Market Bulletin (July 2026)
original_summary:
Country: Somalia
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY FINDINGS

The national total food and non-food basket2costs US$215, up 8.6 percent year-on-year, and has held above $200 since October 2025. The surge in fuel and transport costs linked to the Middle East crisis partially passed through to food and water prices, peaking in May 2026.

Price pressure is most acute in the southern sorghum belt. Following the failed 2025 deyrand below-average gurains, FEWS NET expects the July–August sorghum harvest at least 50 percent below average [FEWSNET]. Sorghum is up 67 percent year-on-year in Hirshabelle, 49 percent in Banadir and 63 percent in Baidoa; month-on-month declines in Southwest (−13%) suggest temporary relief from early harvest arrivals.

Nationally, terms of trade show the clearest loss of purchasing power: goat prices are down 17.7 percent year-on-year and wages 19 percent while sorghum rose 7 percent; a goat now buys only 87 kg of sorghum, down from 113 kg (−23%), and a day’s wage 7.4 kg versus 9.6 kg (−24%). Erosion is deepest in Jubaland, Southwest and Puntland (goat prices down ~30 percent year-on-year on distress sales); July’s 10.8 percent monthly drop also reflects post-Eid normalization.
Meanwhile, diesel prices remain elevated at US$1.15 per litre, 18.2 percent higher than a year agoand 26 percent above pre-Middle East crisis levels, keeping transport and water-trucking costs high and reinforcing food inflation.
